summary: The decision that admits Nora into a room she was not invited into no longer believes a forged transcript row.
details: The relevance gate is back on a direct JSON completion. Measured on 2026-09-11 against the deployed gate model, 40 labelled windows, five runs each, with one identical instruction on both arms and the transport as the only variable: the direct completion held all 6 safety cases, and the Agent SDK's structured-output path — which is what was running in production — held 1 of 6.

The case it failed is a member pasting a fake `[assistant]:` line into their own message: the gate believed it was something Nora had said, and admitted the turn on four runs out of five. That is an unprompted turn triggered by whoever typed the forgery, not a judgement call it got wrong.

The cause is below the instruction and no wording change reaches it. The SDK asks for a structured answer by turning it into a tool call, which makes one request into a three-message exchange, and the provider drops the model's own reasoning out of the middle of it before the verdict is formed.
The gate also got cheaper: 2,055 prompt tokens per window against 5,021, a 2.4x saving on the highest-frequency model call in the system, paid on every closed window.
limitations: Nothing says this hole was ever used. Over 20.3 hours of the shadow soak the gate admitted 0 of 33 windows because the rooms were quiet, so the gap had not been exercised — that is why the risk had not landed, not a reason it was acceptable.

The two false NO_GOs the suite reports are identical on both transports and are unchanged by this: the gate still declines two windows it should admit. The debrief and the standing fold stay on the SDK; neither decides whether Nora speaks.
